why: Every sentence is a dictionary word followed by a sentence for the rest of the string, so the answer for suffix i is built from the answers for later suffixes. Backtracking over split points with memoisation by start index is the standard solution; a trie can speed up the 'which words start here' lookup, which is the link to this week's Tries topic.
hints: Pick the first word: it must be a dictionary word that is a prefix of s. What remains is the same problem on a shorter string.
Define sentences(i) = every way to split s[i:]. For each j where s[i:j] is a word, prepend it to each sentence in sentences(j). sentences(n) = [''] (one empty way).
Memoise on i (lru_cache) so each suffix is solved once; only try lengths up to the longest word. Sort the final list. Output-sensitive time, fine for |s| <= 20.
pitfalls: Return the sentences in lexicographic order.
When no segmentation exists return [], and avoid emitting a trailing space for the last word.
statement:
Given a string s and a list of distinct dictionary words wordDict, insert spaces into s so that every piece is a dictionary word. Return every possible resulting sentence, sorted lexicographically. Words may be used any number of times. Return [] if no split works.

Worked example. s = "catsanddog", wordDict = ["cat","cats","and","sand","dog"].

  • Prefixes of s in the dictionary: "cat" and "cats".
  • After "cat" the rest is "sanddog": "sand" then "dog" works, giving cat sand dog.
  • After "cats" the rest is "anddog": "and" then "dog" works, giving cats and dog.
  • Sorted: ["cat sand dog", "cats and dog"].
